term: Verifying a custom domain in Microsoft 365
def: You add the custom domain in the admin center, then Microsoft 365 gives you a unique TXT record value to add at your DNS host. Once the TXT record is published and detected, the domain is verified and you can add MX, CNAME (Autodiscover), and SPF records to route mail and enable services.
eg: Domain verification only proves ownership; it does not by itself move mail flow. You still have to update MX records at the DNS host to actually route mail through Exchange Online.

def: Group-based licensing assigns a license to a Microsoft Entra security group, and every current and future member of that group automatically inherits it. Direct licensing assigns a license to one user at a time and must be repeated for each new hire or role change.
eg: Group-based licensing scales far better for onboarding/offboarding at volume, since adding or removing a user from the group is the only step needed — no separate license action.

term: Disabling an individual service plan within a license
def: A license SKU (like Microsoft 365 E3) bundles many service plans (Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Viva Engage, Stream, etc.). An admin can disable specific service plans for a user or group while keeping the rest of the license active, instead of removing the whole license.
eg: This is how you grant everything else in a bundle while withholding one workload a user should not have — for example, disabling the Viva Engage service plan (formerly Yammer) for a group that should not use it.

def: GDAP lets a Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) partner be granted only the specific, time-bound Microsoft Entra roles it needs to support a customer tenant, following least-privilege principles. It replaced the older partner-access model, which gave the partner broad Admin Agent access (effectively Global Administrator) across the whole tenant with no expiration.
prompt: _____ lets a Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) partner be granted only the specific, time-bound Microsoft Entra roles it needs to support a customer tenant, following least-privilege principles. It replaced the older partner-access model, which gave the partner broad Admin Agent access (effectively Global Administrator) across the whole tenant with no expiration.
eg: Microsoft deprecated classic Delegated Admin Privileges (DAP) in favor of GDAP and began transitioning and removing DAP relationships in 2023, specifically because DAP's all-or-nothing, non-expiring access violated least-privilege administration.

term: Microsoft 365 Apps update channels: Current, Monthly Enterprise, Semi-Annual Enterprise
def: Current Channel delivers new features to users as soon as they are ready (roughly monthly, with feature updates arriving unpredictably). Monthly Enterprise Channel delivers the same features but bundled once a month on a predictable, fixed release date, the second Tuesday. Semi-Annual Enterprise Channel, meant for devices that need extensive testing, used to receive feature updates only twice a year (January and July); since Version 2606 (July 2026) it is unified with Monthly Enterprise Channel, so those devices get the same monthly feature and security updates.
eg: Microsoft recommends Monthly Enterprise Channel when you want features every month but need to know the release date in advance (the second Tuesday). Semi-Annual Enterprise Channel was the choice for select devices that needed extensive testing; after the Version 2606 unification, devices still configured for it show as Monthly Enterprise Channel in the Office apps.

term: Shared mailbox vs. distribution group vs. Microsoft 365 group
def: A shared mailbox is a single mailbox multiple people can send/receive from with delegated permissions (no license required if under the size limit). A distribution group only routes mail to its members' own inboxes. A Microsoft 365 group is a broader membership object that also provisions a shared mailbox, a SharePoint site, a Planner, and other connected resources.
eg: A common exam trap is treating a distribution group as if it stores mail — it does not; mail sent to it simply fans out to each member's own mailbox.

def: SharePoint external sharing can be set (at the organization level, and then narrowed per site) to Anyone (anonymous links), New and existing guests (requires sign-in or verification), Existing guests only, or Only people in your organization. Each site's sharing level can never be more permissive than the org-wide setting.
eg: This layered model means the org-wide setting acts as a ceiling: tightening it at the tenant level immediately restricts what any individual site admin can allow, regardless of that site's own configuration.

def: Microsoft 365 network endpoints are published as Optimize (highest volume/latency-sensitive, like Teams media and Exchange — should bypass proxies/VPNs), Allow (required but lower priority), and Default (general Microsoft 365 traffic that can be routed like normal internet traffic).
eg: Routing Optimize category endpoints through a traditional on-premises proxy or VPN hairpin is the classic cause of poor Teams call quality, since it adds latency to traffic Microsoft explicitly says should take the most direct path.

def: An Exchange Online tool that follows a specific email through the mail flow pipeline, showing exactly when it was received, what rules or policies acted on it, and where it ended up — delivered, quarantined, or dropped.
eg: This is the first stop for 'did my email actually send/arrive' tickets, before escalating further into Defender for Office 365's Threat Explorer for anything security-related.

def: Exchange Online rules that inspect messages in transit and take an action — add a disclaimer, redirect, block, or apply encryption — based on conditions like sender, recipient, or message content.
eg: A Message trace shows what actually happened to one message after the fact; a mail flow rule is what decides what happens to messages matching a condition going forward.

term: Domain reuse during a tenant-to-tenant migration
def: A custom domain can only be verified in one Microsoft 365 tenant at a time, so before it can be added and reverified in a destination tenant it must first be removed from the source tenant's verified domains. Until the domain's DNS records are cut over to the destination tenant, mail addressed to that domain continues routing to the source tenant.
eg: Because removing the domain from the source tenant immediately stops it from accepting mail there, the domain cutover is normally planned as the last, tightly timed step of a migration — after mailbox content and permissions have already landed in the destination tenant.

term: Least-privilege delegation with built-in Microsoft 365 admin roles
def: Built-in roles like Helpdesk Administrator, User Administrator, License Administrator, and Exchange Administrator grant narrower, task-specific rights than Global Administrator, letting front-line staff perform routine actions (like resetting a non-admin user's password) without tenant-wide control. Custom Microsoft Entra roles can narrow permissions even further when no built-in role fits exactly.
eg: Helpdesk Administrator can reset passwords only for non-administrators and other Helpdesk Administrators — a scenario asking who can reset a Global Administrator's forgotten password is pointing at a higher-privilege role or the affected admin's own recovery options, not Helpdesk Administrator.

term: Service health vs. Message center in the Microsoft 365 admin center
def: Service health reports the real-time operational status of each Microsoft 365 service — active incidents, advisories, and resolution timelines — so admins can confirm whether a problem is a known Microsoft-side issue. Message center instead posts upcoming and recently rolled-out changes, new features, and deprecations that admins need to plan for, independent of whether anything is currently broken.
eg: A user reporting that a familiar feature suddenly "looks different" or "stopped working" is often not an outage at all — checking Message center for a recently announced feature rollout explains many such tickets that Service health will show nothing for.

term: Microsoft Entra Connect vs. Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync
def: Microsoft Entra Connect is a full-featured, server-based sync engine that supports complex custom sync rules and can synchronize multiple connected forests, but it takes more hands-on management. Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync instead uses lightweight agents managed mostly from the cloud and can run several agents at once, which more easily syncs multiple, even disconnected, on-premises AD forests into one tenant, though it supports a narrower feature set than Connect.
eg: Cloud Sync's ability to run lightweight agents inside each forest makes it the simpler choice for a merger or acquisition with disconnected AD forests, while Entra Connect's richer sync engine is usually preferred when an organization needs advanced features such as complex custom attribute-filtering rules.

term: Email authentication: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC
def: SPF publishes a DNS TXT record listing which mail servers are authorized to send on behalf of a domain. DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to each outgoing message, verified against a public key published in DNS. DMARC tells receiving servers what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail — monitor, quarantine, or reject — and where to send aggregate failure reports.
eg: DMARC is the layer that actually sets a disposition and generates reporting; SPF and DKIM only establish whether a message passes authentication, neither one alone says what a receiving server should then do about a failure.

term: Usage location on a user account
def: Usage location is a required attribute on a user's profile that determines which licenses and services can legally be assigned to them, since some countries and regions have service availability restrictions. A license cannot be assigned directly to a user whose profile has no usage location set.
eg: Group-based licensing is more forgiving but not a safe shortcut: a group member with no usage location inherits the location of the tenant, so services could be assigned for the wrong country. Set usage location when the user is created.

def: A dynamic group (security or Microsoft 365 group) automatically adds or removes members based on a membership rule evaluated against attributes like department or job title, instead of someone manually curating the member list by hand.
eg: This is what lets group-based licensing scale with no manual membership upkeep, since the group's own membership stays current on its own as attributes change.

term: Global Reader vs. Reports Reader admin roles
def: Global Reader grants read-only visibility into nearly every admin center and configuration setting a Global Administrator could view, with no edit rights at all, which suits an auditor. Reports Reader grants a much narrower read-only view, limited specifically to usage reports and reporting dashboards.
eg: This is least-privilege delegation applied to oversight: Global Reader exists specifically so an auditor never needs standing edit rights just to review configuration end to end.

def: Multi-Geo lets a single tenant store a given user's primary mailbox, OneDrive, and SharePoint data in a geographic region of choice (a satellite location), while the organization remains one tenant with one directory, instead of operating a fully separate tenant per region.
eg: This differs from the EU Data Boundary, which governs whether an entire in-scope tenant's data (including Copilot data processing) stays within the EU/EFTA region — Multi-Geo instead controls where a given user's own data physically sits within one tenant spanning several regions.

def: Meeting policies control what participants can do in Teams meetings — recording, transcription, who can present. Messaging policies control chat capabilities — editing or deleting sent messages, stickers and Giphy. Both are assigned per user or group, and policy packages bundle several related policies together for a role like Frontline Worker.
eg: This is a workload-configuration control, not an identity-layer one — a user needing different meeting behavior gets a different Teams policy assigned, not a change to a Conditional Access policy.

term: Self-service password reset (SSPR) registration vs. reset method counts
def: SSPR lets an admin set how many authentication methods a user must provide to reset a password (one or two), and users must register at least that many methods. Encouraging users to register more methods than a reset requires — for example, three registered methods with one needed at reset — means a user who loses access to one method can still recover their account.
prompt: _____ lets an admin set how many authentication methods a user must provide to reset a password (one or two), and users must register at least that many methods. Encouraging users to register more methods than a reset requires — for example, three registered methods with one needed at reset — means a user who loses access to one method can still recover their account.
eg: Having only the bare minimum of methods registered creates a single point of failure: lose that one method and self-service reset becomes impossible, forcing a helpdesk-assisted reset instead.

term: Microsoft 365 Groups naming policy and blocked words
def: A groups naming policy can enforce a prefix or suffix convention (like dept- or -grp) on every new Microsoft 365 group and Team, and separately maintain a blocked words list that rejects group names containing specific terms (like executive titles or offensive language) at creation time.
eg: This keeps self-service group creation from producing confusingly named or impersonation-prone groups and Teams at scale, without requiring an admin to manually review every group name as it's created.

term: Teams external access (federation) vs. guest access
def: External access (federation) lets users in one organization's tenant chat, call, and meet with users in another organization's tenant without either side becoming a member of the other's tenant. Guest access instead adds an external user as an actual Microsoft Entra B2B guest member of a specific team, giving them persistent access to that team's channels, files, and apps.
eg: A vendor who should be able to message your employees occasionally needs external access; a long-term contractor who needs to sit inside one specific Team's channels and files day after day needs to be added as a guest instead.

def: A service in the Microsoft 365 Apps admin center that enforces Office policy settings, much like Group Policy, on Microsoft 365 Apps wherever a targeted user signs in, even on devices that are not domain joined or otherwise managed.
eg: Policies apply to users and Microsoft Entra groups, not devices. The Allow web search in Copilot policy is one of the settings an admin can configure here.

def: Containers that subdivide a tenant so a role assignment can be limited to the users, groups, or devices inside that unit instead of applying tenant-wide. They let you delegate administration without granting broad rights.
eg: A Helpdesk Administrator scoped to the Sales administrative unit can reset passwords only for Sales users and cannot change tenant-wide settings.

def: The most privileged Microsoft Entra role, with access to nearly every administrative feature and the ability to assign any other role. Microsoft recommends fewer than five Global Administrators and using narrower roles for daily work.
eg: Exam angle: when a scenario needs only one task, such as resetting passwords or reading reports, the answer is a least-privilege role, not Global Administrator.

def: User Administrator can create and manage users and groups, assign licenses, and reset passwords for users and some limited admin roles. Helpdesk Administrator can reset passwords and sign users out, but only for non-administrators and other helpdesk admins, and cannot create users.
eg: A support tier that only unlocks accounts needs Helpdesk Administrator. Onboarding staff who must create accounts and assign licenses needs User Administrator.

def: An app registration is the definition of an application in Microsoft Entra ID. A service principal is that app's identity inside a specific tenant, appearing as an enterprise application, where permissions and access are actually granted.
eg: Admins assign permissions and Conditional Access to the service principal. That is why the Copilot sign-in policy targets a service principal rather than an app registration.

def: An on-premises service that provides federated sign-in. With federation, Microsoft Entra ID redirects authentication to it, so passwords are validated by your own infrastructure instead of in the cloud.
eg: It gives the most control but needs servers you must keep highly available. Password hash sync is the simplest hybrid choice, which is why moving off AD FS is a common simplification.

term: Microsoft Entra ID P1 vs. P2
def: P1 adds premium features such as Conditional Access, dynamic groups, and self-service password reset with writeback. P2 includes everything in P1 and adds Microsoft Entra ID Protection with risk-based Conditional Access, plus Privileged Identity Management.
eg: If a scenario needs sign-in risk or user risk policies, or just-in-time admin elevation, the license answer is P2. Basic Conditional Access alone only needs P1.

term: Microsoft 365 Backup: what it protects and how restore works
def: Microsoft 365 Backup protects SharePoint sites, OneDrive accounts and Exchange Online mailboxes. Each workload has its own backup policy, and the recovery window on a policy can be 3 months, 6 months, 1 year or 2 years. SharePoint sites and OneDrive accounts are restored by rolling back to a prior point in time (to the same or a new URL); mailboxes can be restored in full or at item level to the same or a new folder.
eg: It is built for ransomware and mass-deletion recovery at scale, not for long-term compliance retention. Retention policies keep content for legal or regulatory reasons, whereas Backup returns a site, drive or mailbox to a known-good moment.

term: Setting up Microsoft 365 Backup (roles and billing)
def: Setting up Microsoft 365 Backup requires the SharePoint Administrator or Global Administrator role (a dedicated Microsoft 365 Backup Administrator role can then manage the whole tool). Billing is pay-as-you-go through an Azure subscription (you need Owner or Contributor on it, plus a resource group and region), and you pay for the data protected, while restores are not charged. After billing is linked, you create backup policies for OneDrive, SharePoint and Exchange in Settings > Microsoft 365 Backup.
prompt: _____ requires the SharePoint Administrator or Global Administrator role (a dedicated Microsoft 365 Backup Administrator role can then manage the whole tool). Billing is pay-as-you-go through an Azure subscription (you need Owner or Contributor on it, plus a resource group and region), and you pay for the data protected, while restores are not charged. After billing is linked, you create backup policies for OneDrive, SharePoint and Exchange in Settings > Microsoft 365 Backup.
eg: Customers onboarding after April 1, 2026 use the pay-as-you-go setup under the Billing node of the admin center, which adds budget alerts and lets backup costs be split across several Azure subscriptions (departmental billing).

def: Some Microsoft 365 services are not licensed per user but metered against an Azure subscription through pay-as-you-go billing in the Billing node of the Microsoft 365 admin center. Non-Copilot examples include Microsoft 365 Backup, extra SharePoint storage and High Volume Email. An admin creates a billing policy that links an Azure subscription, resource group and region to the service.
eg: A missing or deleted Azure subscription link is a common reason a metered service stops working. Copilot-related consumption is governed separately through spending policies in Copilot Cost management.

term: Custom organization themes in the Microsoft 365 admin center
def: In Settings > Org settings > Organization profile > Custom themes, an admin defines the default theme that everyone sees in the top navigation bar, plus up to four additional group themes. A group theme can be assigned to up to five Microsoft 365 groups, and each theme has General, Logos and Colors tabs (logo images must be reachable over HTTPS, with an alternate logo for dark mode).
eg: The default theme applies to everyone who is not matched by a group theme, and it cannot be renamed or deleted until the other themes are gone. Group themes are how a subsidiary or brand gets its own look inside one tenant.

term: Company branding on the Microsoft Entra sign-in page
def: The sign-in page and Access Panel pages that users see are branded through Microsoft Entra company branding (logo, background image or color, banner text), which is separate from the Microsoft 365 admin center theme that colors the navigation bar once users are inside the apps. Branding can be set per language and applies to the tenant's sign-in experience.
eg: If a question asks where to change what users see before they authenticate, the answer is Entra company branding; if it asks about the in-app header color and logo, it is the organization theme.

term: Network connectivity insights in the Microsoft 365 admin center
def: Health > Network connectivity shows network assessments and insights collected from the tenant's own clients. Location data comes from one of three sources: Windows Location Services opt-in (off by default, needs at least two Wi-Fi-connected PCs per site with OneDrive for Windows), admin-added locations with LAN subnets, or results of the Microsoft 365 network connectivity test run at an office. Reports Reader can view it; Service Support Administrator configures it.
eg: It is not available in GCC Moderate, GCC High or DoD tenants. Because fixes happen at specific offices, the page is organized by location, not just a tenant-wide average.

def: A network assessment condenses TCP latency, download speed and UDP connection quality into a score from 0 to 100, compiled daily, excluding Microsoft-owned networks so the result reflects the customer's own network design. A score of 80 is the healthy baseline where regular user complaints should not occur; 60 is acceptable and 40 or below means users might experience issues. History for the past 30 days is shown.
eg: The score is evidence for an ISP, WAN or local-breakout conversation: a low score at one office points to that office's perimeter design rather than to a Microsoft 365 service outage (which Service health would show).

def: On the Service health page (Health > Service health), an admin selects Customize > Email to receive notifications of new incidents and status changes for their tenant. Up to two email addresses can be set, with a choice of incidents, advisories or both, and the services to follow; a single issue can also be followed through Manage notifications for this issue. The preference is per admin account. Service Support Administrator and Helpdesk Administrator can view Service health.
eg: Service health tells you about Microsoft-side incidents and advisories affecting your tenant. Message center, by contrast, announces upcoming changes. Reporting a problem you do not see listed is done with Report an issue.

term: Copilot in Teams meetings: organizer options and the transcription policy
def: Organizers choose During and after the meeting, Only during the meeting, or Off for Copilot in a meeting. Only during the meeting relies on temporary speech-to-text that is not saved, while During and after the meeting needs a transcript. Off disables Copilot and also turns off recording and transcription. The tenant transcription policy (AllowTranscription in the Teams meeting policy) interacts with the option: with transcription Off and During and after selected, licensed users cannot use Copilot unless another permitted participant starts transcription.
eg: Copilot in Teams meetings needs the Copilot add-on license and is not available in end-to-end encrypted meetings. The admin center shortcut under Copilot > Settings > Copilot actions opens the Teams admin center.

term: Which license enables which AI service
def: Licensing differs by service. Microsoft Copilot is a per-user add-on (included in Microsoft 365 E7) that is assigned to each user, ideally through group-based licensing. Microsoft Agent 365 is licensed per user (included in E7, add-on for E5/A5/Business Premium) and at least one user must hold a qualifying license to enable it. Copilot Studio usage and many agent experiences are billed in Copilot Credits through capacity or pay-as-you-go. Security Copilot is provisioned as Security Compute Units, not per user.
eg: Assigning a license requires a usage location on the user. Owning a SKU in the tenant does nothing for a user until the license is assigned directly or by a group.

term: SharePoint Advanced Management: site lifecycle controls
def: SharePoint Advanced Management (SAM) manages content sprawl with a site ownership policy (minimum owner or admin counts, with notifications), inactive site policies that notify owners, and site attestation requests in which owners confirm a site is still needed and its permissions are right. It also offers catalog management for grouping sites, change history reports covering 180 days and a view of recent site property changes from the last 30 days.
eg: These controls reduce stale, ownerless sites that Copilot would otherwise ground on. SAM is included with a Microsoft Copilot license, which is why it appears in Copilot readiness guidance.

term: SharePoint Advanced Management: block download and Conditional Access for sites
def: SAM lets an admin tie a Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policy to a SharePoint site by using an authentication context, and create a block download policy that prevents moving or downloading files from SharePoint and OneDrive sites and Teams meeting recordings. These sit alongside restricted access control (limit a site to a group) and Restricted Content Discovery (hide a site from search and Copilot).
eg: Choosing the right one depends on the verb in the requirement: hide from search and Copilot, restrict who can open, require a compliant device, or stop downloads each map to a different control.

term: Microsoft Search in SharePoint and Copilot: bookmarks and acronyms
def: Admins curate authoritative answers for Microsoft Search with bookmarks (promote key resources) and acronyms (define internal terminology). The same curated content is used by Microsoft Copilot Search. Microsoft Search in the Microsoft Copilot app is on by default and can be controlled under Settings > Search & intelligence.
eg: Bookmarks and acronyms change what is surfaced for a query, not who has permission to the underlying content.

term: Mail contacts, mail users and guest users
def: A mail contact is an external email address listed in the address book with no sign-in and no mailbox in the tenant. A mail user has a sign-in account in the directory but an external mailbox. A guest user is an external identity invited into the tenant through Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration that can be given access to groups, teams and sites. Contacts are created in the Exchange or Microsoft 365 admin center.
eg: Choose a contact when people only need to find and email someone outside, and a guest when the person must open shared resources.

def: Security defaults are a free, one-size-fits-all baseline (requiring MFA registration for all users, blocking legacy authentication, and similar protections) that cannot be customized. Conditional Access is a licensed (Entra ID P1/P2) policy engine that lets you build granular if-then rules based on user, app, device, location, and risk.
eg: Security defaults and Conditional Access are mutually exclusive per tenant — enabling Conditional Access policies requires turning security defaults off, since Conditional Access is meant to fully replace that baseline with tailored rules.

term: Password hash sync vs. pass-through authentication vs. federation
def: Password hash sync (PHS) synchronizes a hash of the on-premises password hash to Microsoft Entra ID so sign-in is validated in the cloud. Pass-through authentication (PTA) validates the password directly against on-premises Active Directory via lightweight agents, with no password hash stored in the cloud. Federation (e.g., AD FS) delegates authentication entirely to an external identity provider.
eg: Microsoft recommends password hash sync (often paired with seamless SSO) as the default hybrid identity method for most organizations, since it is the simplest to operate and, because the hashes reach Entra ID, it also enables leaked-credential detection in Entra ID Protection and works as a fallback if on-premises authentication is unavailable.

term: Conditional Access grant controls vs. session controls
def: Grant controls decide whether access is allowed at all, and under what conditions (require MFA, require a compliant device, require a hybrid Microsoft Entra joined device, block access). Session controls apply restrictions during an already-granted session (like Conditional Access App Control through Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, app enforced restrictions, or limiting sign-in frequency).
eg: A policy can combine both: grant access only if MFA is satisfied (a grant control), then also restrict that session to browser-only, no-download access (a session control) for an unmanaged device.

term: Defender for Office 365: Safe Links vs. Safe Attachments
def: Safe Links rewrites URLs in email and Office documents so that each click is checked against threat intelligence at the time of click, not just at delivery time. Safe Attachments detonates attachments in an isolated sandbox environment before delivery to catch malware that static scanning would miss.
eg: Safe Links' time-of-click protection is what defeats a delayed-activation phishing link — one that was clean when the email arrived but was weaponized by the attacker afterward.

term: Microsoft Defender XDR unified incident correlation
def: Microsoft Defender XDR correlates signals across Defender for Office 365, Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Identity, and Defender for Cloud Apps into a single unified incident in the Microsoft Defender portal, instead of leaving admins to manually connect related alerts from each product separately.
eg: An exam scenario describing an attack that touches email, an endpoint, and identity sign-in behavior is pointing at the unified incident view in Defender XDR as the place to investigate the full attack chain in one place.

def: A Microsoft Purview DLP policy defines locations (Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams chat, endpoint devices), conditions that detect sensitive content (like matching a sensitive information type such as a credit card number), and actions/rules (block sharing, show a policy tip, restrict access, or require an override justification).
prompt: A Microsoft Purview _____ policy defines locations (Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams chat, endpoint devices), conditions that detect sensitive content (like matching a sensitive information type such as a credit card number), and actions/rules (block sharing, show a policy tip, restrict access, or require an override justification).
eg: DLP policies can run in simulation mode first (with or without policy tips shown to users) before being enforced, which is the recommended way to tune false positives before the policy starts blocking real business activity.

def: A retention policy applies the same retain/delete rule broadly across a whole location (a mailbox, a SharePoint site, a Teams channel) without users needing to do anything. A retention label is applied to individual items (by a user or automatically via a trainable classifier or sensitive-info match) so different content in the same location can have different retention behavior.
eg: When a policy and a label disagree about how long to keep an item, the longer retention period generally wins, and an explicit "retain" instruction generally wins over a "delete" instruction — content is preserved by default when rules conflict.

def: A sensitivity label classifies and protects content itself — it can apply encryption, add a watermark or header/footer, and restrict permissions, and it travels with the file. A retention label governs the lifecycle of the content — how long it must be kept or when it must be deleted — and does not by itself add any protection to the content.
eg: The two are independent and can both be applied to the same document at once: a sensitivity label encrypting it as "Confidential" while a separate retention label governs when it can eventually be deleted.

def: eDiscovery (Standard) lets you create cases, search content across locations, and export results for basic legal hold and search scenarios. eDiscovery Premium (part of Microsoft Purview) adds custodian management, legal hold notifications, advanced review sets, analytics (near-duplicate detection, email threading, themes), and review workflow features for complex litigation.
eg: A scenario describing custodian communications, hold notifications, or analytics like near-duplicate/threading is pointing specifically at Premium — Standard search-and-export alone cannot do custodian-level workflow.

def: Insider Risk Management uses signals (like unusual file downloads, mass deletions, or data exfiltration to personal accounts) combined with HR data (such as resignation or termination events) to surface and score potentially risky internal user activity, while pseudonymization keeps reviewers from seeing unnecessary personal detail.
prompt: _____ uses signals (like unusual file downloads, mass deletions, or data exfiltration to personal accounts) combined with HR data (such as resignation or termination events) to surface and score potentially risky internal user activity, while pseudonymization keeps reviewers from seeing unnecessary personal detail.
eg: Pseudonymization of user identities in case alerts, until an investigator explicitly needs to reveal them, is a specific control meant to balance risk detection against employee privacy during the review process.

def: Communication compliance scans internal and external communications (email, Teams chats, third-party connectors) for policy violations like harassment, sensitive data sharing, or regulatory language, routing flagged items to reviewers instead of blocking the message outright.
prompt: _____ scans internal and external communications (email, Teams chats, third-party connectors) for policy violations like harassment, sensitive data sharing, or regulatory language, routing flagged items to reviewers instead of blocking the message outright.
eg: Unlike DLP, communication compliance is a detect-and-review workflow, not a real-time block — it is meant to surface conduct and compliance risk for human review, not to stop a message from sending.

def: Audit (Standard) retains audit records for 180 days by default and covers a broad set of crucial events across Microsoft 365 services. Audit (Premium) builds on it with audit log retention policies, retention of up to one year by default for E5-licensed users (up to ten years with an add-on), intelligent insights, and higher bandwidth access to the Office 365 Management Activity API.
eg: An investigation asking exactly which items in a mailbox were read after a suspected compromise needs the "MailItemsAccessed" event. Microsoft rolled that event (along with Send) out to Audit (Standard) in 2024, so the deciding factor in scenarios is usually retention: Standard's 180 days versus Premium's one year.

def: Information barriers are Microsoft Purview policies that explicitly restrict which users or groups can communicate and collaborate with each other in Teams and OneDrive/SharePoint, used to prevent conflicts of interest (for example, keeping an investment banking team from chatting with a research team).
prompt: _____ are Microsoft Purview policies that explicitly restrict which users or groups can communicate and collaborate with each other in Teams and OneDrive/SharePoint, used to prevent conflicts of interest (for example, keeping an investment banking team from chatting with a research team).
eg: Information barriers actively block communication and content discovery between defined segments, which makes them a different kind of control from Conditional Access, which governs the conditions for signing in rather than who can talk to whom.

def: A measurement of an organization's security posture, expressed as a numeric score, based on completed security actions (like enabling MFA or turning on a Conditional Access policy) weighed against recommended improvement actions across identity, devices, apps, and data.
eg: Secure Score recommendations link directly to the admin console page needed to implement them, and the score updates automatically as configuration changes are detected, rather than needing a manual re-scan trigger.

def: Compliance Manager translates regulatory and internal-policy requirements into actionable improvement actions, tracked as a compliance score, and distinguishes Microsoft-managed actions (already fulfilled by the service) from your-responsibility actions that your organization must implement and attest to.
eg: The split between Microsoft-managed and customer-managed actions reflects the shared responsibility model — Microsoft attests to its own controls, but a customer-responsibility action (like configuring a DLP policy) still needs your organization to implement and document it.

term: Role-based access control (RBAC) in Microsoft Purview
def: Purview permissions can be granted through role groups (built-in, like Compliance Administrator, or custom) in addition to Microsoft Entra roles, letting you grant scoped access to specific compliance solutions (like eDiscovery or DLP) without granting broader Microsoft 365 admin rights.
eg: A user can hold zero Microsoft Entra admin roles and still fully manage DLP policies, because Purview role groups are a separate permission layer purpose-built for compliance solutions.

def: A Microsoft Purview tool showing exactly which items across the tenant currently carry a given sensitivity label or match specific sensitive information types, letting an admin see the real scope of sensitive content before or after rolling out a policy.
eg: This is where you'd confirm that the sensitive information types or labels a DLP policy relies on actually match the content you think they do, rather than assuming from the policy definition alone.

term: Sensitivity label scopes: Files & emails vs. Groups & sites
def: A sensitivity label scoped to Files & emails protects individual documents and messages with encryption, watermarks, headers/footers, and permission restrictions. A label scoped to Groups & sites instead applies container-level settings to a Microsoft 365 Group, Team, or SharePoint site itself — controlling its privacy (public/private), external user access, and unmanaged device access.
eg: A label meant to lock down an entire Team's privacy and guest access must have its Groups & sites scope enabled — the Files & emails scope alone never touches container-level settings, even if it is the only scope an admin remembers to turn on when publishing the label.

term: DLP policy and rule priority (evaluation order)
def: Microsoft Purview DLP policies are evaluated in priority order, where a lower priority number is evaluated first, and within a policy its rules are evaluated top-down. When a rule's conditions match and its action includes "stop processing more rules," later lower-priority rules and policies are skipped for that item.
eg: When two overlapping DLP policies appear to give conflicting results on the same content, the fix is usually reordering policy priority rather than editing either policy's conditions, since priority — not creation date — decides which policy's action actually applies.

term: Risk-based Conditional Access: sign-in risk vs. user risk
def: Microsoft Entra ID Protection feeds Conditional Access two distinct risk signals: sign-in risk, a real-time, session-specific signal (like an impossible-travel pattern or an anonymous IP), and user risk, an ongoing aggregate likelihood that the account itself is compromised (such as a leaked-credential match). Policies can require different responses for each, like MFA for elevated sign-in risk versus a secure password change for high user risk.
eg: The two risk types remediate differently: satisfying MFA for one risky sign-in clears that session's sign-in risk, but it does not clear high user risk from leaked credentials — that typically requires the user to actually change their password.

term: Who can search the Microsoft Purview audit log

def: Access reviews let an admin schedule periodic, recurring recertification of who still needs a given assignment — a role activated through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM), a security group membership, or a guest's access to a resource — requiring a reviewer to explicitly approve or deny continued access instead of it persisting indefinitely by default.

term: Admin consent workflow and app consent policies
def: App consent policies control whether a user can consent on their own to let a third-party or custom app access organizational data through Microsoft Graph permissions, or whether such requests must instead be routed to an admin through the admin consent workflow for explicit approval.
eg: This governs the same kind of permission-granting exposure that an ungoverned Copilot agent or plugin could otherwise exploit — requiring admin consent closes the gap where a user could unknowingly approve broad Graph access just to install a convenient add-in.

term: Records Management: regulatory records vs. standard retention labels
def: A standard retention label still lets an authorized user remove the label or, in some configurations, edit the underlying content. Declaring an item a regulatory record through Microsoft Purview Records Management locks it down so that even its label and key properties can't be changed or removed by anyone, including an admin, until its retention period genuinely runs out.
eg: This is the item-level counterpart of Preservation Lock, which protects a whole retention policy — once an item is declared a regulatory record, the restriction stays in force until the retention period ends, and an administrator cannot simply remove it.

def: A service that detects identity risks, such as risky sign-ins and risky users, using signals like leaked credentials, impossible travel, and anonymous IP addresses. It feeds those risk levels into Conditional Access for automatic responses. It needs Microsoft Entra ID P2.
eg: A user flagged with high user risk can be forced to change their password, while a risky sign-in can require MFA. The signal drives the policy, not the other way around.

def: A cloud access security broker that discovers which cloud apps people use, controls access and sessions to them, and detects unusual activity. Session controls work through Conditional Access to limit what users can do inside an app.
eg: Blocking downloads of labeled files from an unmanaged device, while still allowing browser viewing, is a classic session-policy use case.

term: Microsoft Defender for Office 365 plans (Plan 1 and Plan 2)
def: Plan 1 gives preventive protection: Safe Links, Safe Attachments, and anti-phishing with impersonation detection. Plan 2 adds investigation and response, including Threat Explorer, automated investigation and response (AIR), campaigns, and Attack simulation training.
eg: A scenario that asks to hunt for a phishing message across mailboxes, or to remediate it automatically, needs Plan 2. Blocking bad links at click time is already Plan 1.

def: Older sign-in methods, such as IMAP, POP, SMTP AUTH, and some older Office clients using basic authentication, that cannot perform multifactor authentication. Attackers use them for password spray because MFA cannot stop them.
eg: Security defaults block legacy authentication automatically. With Conditional Access, you create a policy that blocks it yourself.

def: When approving a sign-in in the Microsoft Authenticator app, the user must type a number shown on the sign-in screen into the app. This makes it much harder to approve a request by accident or under pressure.
eg: It counters MFA fatigue, where an attacker floods a user with push prompts hoping for one tap. A plain approve button gives no proof the user started the sign-in.

def: A time-limited passcode issued by an admin that lets a user sign in without a password to register passwordless methods, such as a FIDO2 key or Authenticator, or to recover access. It can be set as one-time use or multi-use.
eg: Use it for a new hire's first sign-in or a user who lost their phone. It bootstraps passwordless credentials without ever giving a permanent password.

def: A policy state that evaluates a Conditional Access policy for each sign-in and logs what would have happened, without enforcing it. Admins review the results before turning the policy on.
eg: Putting a new block-by-location policy in report-only first reveals which legitimate users it would lock out. It is the safe way to test before enforcement.

def: Defined sets of IP address ranges, or countries and regions, that a Conditional Access policy can use as a condition. A named location can be marked trusted, such as an office network.
eg: Require MFA for every sign-in except from the trusted office range, or block sign-ins from countries where the company has no staff. Both use named locations.

def: Pattern-based detectors for data like credit card or national ID numbers, using regular expressions, keywords, checksums, and a confidence level. Microsoft Purview uses them in DLP, auto-labeling, and retention.
eg: Use a SIT when data has a recognizable format. For documents defined by their content rather than a pattern, a trainable classifier is the better tool.

def: Machine learning models that recognize a category of content, such as contracts or source code, by learning from sample documents instead of matching a pattern. Microsoft provides built-in ones, and you can train your own.
eg: A SIT finds a credit card number. A trainable classifier recognizes a whole document as, say, a financial statement and can then drive a label or retention policy.

def: Extends Microsoft Purview DLP to files on onboarded Windows and macOS devices, so admins can audit or restrict actions such as copying to USB, uploading to cloud services, printing, or copying to the clipboard.
eg: Preventing a labeled file from going to a USB drive needs Endpoint DLP. Exchange and SharePoint DLP locations cannot see what happens on a local device.

term: DLP policy tips and user overrides
def: A policy tip is a notice in the app telling a user that content conflicts with a DLP policy. An override lets the user proceed after giving a business justification or reporting a false positive, and the action is still logged.
eg: A rule in simulation mode with tips off collects data silently. Allowing overrides keeps work moving but still records who bypassed the rule and why.

def: A hidden library in a SharePoint site or OneDrive where Microsoft Purview keeps a copy of the original of any item changed or deleted while subject to retention. The copy stays until the retention period ends.
eg: A user deletes a contract that is under a retention policy: it vanishes from the site but remains in the Preservation Hold library. It is for retention and eDiscovery, not user recovery.

def: A hidden Exchange mailbox folder that holds deleted items and retained copies for holds and retention. Teams and Copilot interaction data under retention is kept in its SubstrateHolds subfolder.
eg: A litigation hold on a mailbox keeps items here even after the user empties Deleted Items. It is the Exchange counterpart of the Preservation Hold library.

def: A Microsoft Purview feature linking Insider Risk Management with DLP. It assigns users an insider risk level of elevated, moderate, or minor and applies stricter DLP controls to higher-risk users, relaxing them as risk drops.
eg: Instead of blocking everyone, a policy can apply tough restrictions only to users whose behavior has raised their risk level, so low-risk users keep working normally.

term: Microsoft Entra Password Protection: global and custom banned password lists
def: Entra Password Protection checks every password change or reset against a global banned password list that Microsoft maintains automatically from Entra telemetry (it cannot be disabled and its contents are not published) and an optional custom banned password list of up to 1,000 organization-specific base terms such as brand, product and location names. Fuzzy matching and substitution handling block variants, so only the base terms need listing.
eg: Add the base term, not every variation: 'Contoso' covers 'Contoso!1' and similar. The custom list needs Microsoft Entra ID P1.

term: Entra Password Protection for on-premises Active Directory
def: Extending Password Protection to AD DS uses a DC agent installed on domain controllers (a password filter DLL plus service) and a Password Protection proxy service on a domain-joined server that forwards policy downloads from Entra ID. Domain controllers never contact the internet, no schema changes or new ports are required, and password hash sync is not needed. The policy applies only where the DC agent runs, so it should be on every domain controller.
eg: Partial deployment is supported for testing but is not secure, because a client can change its password through a DC that lacks the agent.

def: The Authentication methods policy (Entra ID > Authentication methods > Policies, managed by at least the Authentication Policy Administrator) is the recommended place to enable methods such as Microsoft Authenticator, FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, Temporary Access Pass and SMS for specific groups. The legacy per-tenant MFA and SSPR method settings could no longer manage authentication methods after September 30, 2025. Authentication strengths can then require specific method combinations in Conditional Access.

term: SSPR requirements: registration, number of methods and writeback
def: For self-service password reset, users must be in scope and have registered the required number of methods (one or two, set by the admin). Administrator accounts always use a strong two-method reset policy regardless of tenant settings. If a user's password is mastered in on-premises AD (synchronized, pass-through or federated), SSPR works only when password writeback is configured; otherwise the user is told to contact the admin.
eg: Admin roles are always held to the stronger two-method policy even if the tenant policy only requires one, so test SSPR with a standard user, not an administrator.

term: External collaboration settings for guest users
def: Microsoft Entra external collaboration settings control who can invite guests (for example members only, admins and the Guest Inviter role, or anyone), what guests can see in the directory (guest user access restrictions, limited by default), and which domains guests may come from via an allow or deny list. These apply to B2B collaboration and are separate from SharePoint external sharing and Teams external access.
eg: A guest can be blocked at several layers (Entra, SharePoint, Teams). When an invitation fails or a guest cannot reach a resource, check each layer.

def: Cross-tenant access settings define inbound and outbound B2B collaboration and B2B direct connect behavior with specific partner organizations. They let an admin accept the partner's MFA and device compliance claims, so a guest does not have to satisfy MFA twice, and can limit which users, groups and apps are reachable.

term: Bulk user management with Microsoft Graph PowerShell
def: Microsoft Graph PowerShell connects with Connect-MgGraph and the scopes needed, such as User.ReadWrite.All, then uses cmdlets like Get-MgUser, New-MgUser and Update-MgUser, usually driven from Import-Csv for bulk work. The Microsoft Entra admin center also offers CSV templates for bulk create, bulk invite and bulk delete operations. The older MSOnline and Azure AD PowerShell modules are retired and should not be used for new scripts.
eg: Asking for the least privilege applies to scripts too: request only the Graph permission scopes the task needs and sign in with an account holding a suitable role.

term: Defender for Office 365 preset security policies
def: Preset security policies apply Microsoft's recommended settings without per-setting tuning: Standard protection, Strict protection and Built-in protection. Built-in protection gives baseline Safe Links and Safe Attachments coverage to users who are not in Standard, Strict or a custom policy. Standard and Strict are off until an admin turns them on and chooses recipients (users, groups or domains). They are found under Email & collaboration > Policies & rules > Threat policies > Preset security policies in the Microsoft Defender portal.
eg: Preset policies take precedence over custom threat policies for the users they cover, so adding a user to Strict overrides a custom anti-phishing policy for that user.

term: Anti-phishing, anti-spam and anti-malware threat policies
def: Threat policies in the Defender portal include anti-phishing (impersonation protection for users and domains, mailbox intelligence and spoof intelligence), anti-spam, anti-malware, Safe Links and Safe Attachments. Exchange Online Protection supplies anti-spam and anti-malware for every mailbox; Defender for Office 365 adds Safe Links, Safe Attachments and advanced anti-phishing.
eg: Priority accounts get extra visibility and tagging for executives who are targeted, but the protection itself comes from the policies applied to them.

term: Alert policies and alerts in Defender for Office 365
def: Alert policies define activities or threats that raise an alert, with a category and severity. Default policies cover common detections, and admins can add custom policies. Alerts appear in the Defender portal and correlate into incidents in Microsoft Defender XDR so one attack is investigated as a single story rather than as separate email, endpoint and identity alerts.
eg: Triage starts from the incident, then drills into the alert's evidence such as the message, URL or user, and uses Threat Explorer in Plan 2.

def: AIR, part of Defender for Office 365 Plan 2, starts an automated investigation when certain alerts fire, such as a user-reported phish or a malicious URL click. It collects evidence, assesses the threat and proposes remediation (for example soft-deleting messages or blocking senders) for an approver to accept or reject.

def: In Defender for Office 365 Plan 2, attack simulation training lets admins launch simulated phishing using techniques such as credential harvest, malware attachment, link in attachment, link to malware and drive-by URL, and then assign training to users who fall for them. Training campaigns assign training modules without a simulation. Results and repeat-offender data show who needs more training.
eg: A simulation only tests behavior; the training assignment is what changes it, so exam scenarios often pair a simulation with an automatic training follow-up.

term: Data Security Posture Management (DSPM): current vs classic
def: The current Microsoft Purview experience for assessing and improving data security covers Microsoft 365, Azure, Fabric and integrated third-party platforms, and organizes work around data security objectives such as preventing data exposure in Microsoft 365 Copilot interactions and preventing oversharing. It supersedes two earlier experiences, which remain available as classic versions but no longer receive new features.
eg: The classic experiences are DSPM for AI (classic) and DSPM (classic). When an older exam or article says DSPM for AI, the current product's equivalent is DSPM with AI observability and Copilot-focused objectives.

term: DSPM AI observability and data risk assessments
def: AI observability in DSPM shows activity from AI apps and agents, such as oversharing, exfiltration and unusual access patterns, across Microsoft and third-party environments. In DSPM for AI (classic), a weekly data risk assessment automatically runs on the top 100 SharePoint sites by usage, and custom assessments can be added, to find overshared content before or during a Copilot rollout.
eg: These tools find and quantify risk; enforcement still comes from sensitivity labels, DLP policies and SharePoint Advanced Management actions.

term: Reviewing and responding to DLP alerts
def: DLP rules can be configured to generate alerts, with severity thresholds and optional email notification to admins. Admins review the alert in the Microsoft Purview portal or the Microsoft Defender portal, where it can join a Defender XDR incident, look at the matched content and policy, and use Activity explorer to see what happened to the item. User overrides and false positives are used to tune the rule.
eg: Alert volume is a tuning signal: very high volume with mostly overrides suggests conditions that are too broad, while no alerts may mean the policy is only in simulation mode.

def: Microsoft 365 Copilot (now called Microsoft Copilot in Microsoft documentation) requires an eligible base subscription (such as Microsoft 365 E3/E5, Business Standard/Premium, or A3/A5) plus the Copilot add-on license assigned to each user; Microsoft 365 E7 includes it. Simply owning the base subscription does not grant Copilot access on its own.
eg: Because Copilot is an add-on rather than a standalone SKU, group-based licensing is the recommended way to roll it out to a pilot group or department cleanly, the same as any other add-on license.

term: Microsoft 365 Copilot and the Semantic Index
def: The Semantic Index is a Microsoft Graph-based, encrypted index of an organization's content and relationships (files, emails, chats, meetings) that Copilot uses to understand context and ground its responses in organizational data, going beyond simple keyword search.
eg: Because results from the Semantic Index are trimmed to content the requesting user already has permission to access, it is a grounding mechanism, not an access-granting one — it cannot surface content the user could not already open.

term: Copilot respects existing permissions (no new access is granted)
def: Microsoft 365 Copilot only surfaces organizational content in its responses that the requesting user already has at least view permission to, honoring the same permissions model as SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange. Copilot does not grant any new access a user did not already have.
eg: This is exactly why pre-existing oversharing (files broadly shared with "Anyone" or "Everyone except external users" links) becomes a real risk with Copilot — it surfaces what already-overshared access allows, rather than creating a new vulnerability itself.

term: Restricted SharePoint Search and oversharing remediation
def: Restricted SharePoint Search limits organization-wide search and Copilot to an admin-curated allowed list of sites (up to 100), so sites left off the list drop out of those results without any change to user permissions. It was designed as a temporary mitigation while a broader oversharing review is completed. Microsoft has announced its retirement (new enablement blocked from July 31, 2026; fully retired January 31, 2027) and recommends Restricted Content Discovery, which hides individual sites instead.
eg: This is a search-visibility control, not a permissions control — a user who already has direct access to a site that is not on the allowed list can still open it directly, and content the user owns, recently opened, or had shared directly may still be discoverable.

term: Data Security Posture Management for AI (DSPM for AI)

The user's own file access is unaffected.

term: Insider risk management for AI interactions
def: Insider Risk Management can include AI-specific indicators, such as risky or policy-violating prompts submitted to Copilot or other generative AI tools, as signals contributing to a user's overall risk score, alongside traditional indicators like file exfiltration.

term: Auditing and eDiscovery for Copilot interactions
def: Microsoft 365 Copilot prompts and responses are captured as audit log events and can be searched, exported, and placed on legal hold through Microsoft Purview eDiscovery, just like other Microsoft 365 content, giving compliance teams visibility into what users asked Copilot and what it returned.
eg: This audit trail is what makes Copilot interactions discoverable in litigation or an internal investigation — an interaction is treated as a compliance-relevant record, not an ephemeral, unlogged exchange.

term: Responsible AI oversight of AI agents in the tenant

def: Copilot usage reports in the Microsoft 365 admin center, alongside the Viva Insights Copilot Dashboard, show adoption metrics like active users, which apps Copilot is used in, and usage trends over time, letting admins measure rollout success and spot licensed users who are not adopting Copilot.

term: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat vs. licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot
def: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat (now Microsoft Copilot Chat; the evolution of Bing Chat Enterprise) is included at no extra cost with any Microsoft Entra work account and provides web-grounded chat with some limited file-grounded help. The fully licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on goes further, grounding responses in the organization's own Semantic Index across emails, files, and chats, and embedding Copilot directly inside apps like Word, Excel, and Outlook.
eg: Because Copilot Chat is available to nearly every user by default, an organization that has purchased zero Copilot add-on licenses can still have employees genuinely "using Copilot" — governance and DLP planning need to account for this free tier too, not only the paid add-on.

term: Governing Copilot extensibility: plugins and published agents
def: Admins control which third-party plugins, Copilot connectors, and published Copilot agents are available tenant-wide through the agent management settings of the Copilot Control System in the Microsoft 365 admin center (the Agents area of the admin center), letting them allow, block, or scope specific extensions to designated groups instead of leaving extensibility ungoverned.
eg: Publishing a custom agent in Copilot Studio does not by itself make it available tenant-wide — an admin's approval and deployment settings in agent management are often what actually gate whether other users can find and use it, not the act of publishing.

term: Copilot Studio message capacity and pay-as-you-go billing
def: Copilot Studio agent usage draws first from prepaid capacity (capacity packs bought for the tenant), and once that allotment is exhausted, additional usage is billed on a metered, pay-as-you-go basis if enabled, or the agent may stop responding until the next capacity period if it is not. Copilot Studio meters usage in Copilot Credits (formerly called messages), while internal agents used by people who hold a Microsoft 365 Copilot license are covered by that license.
eg: A heavily used custom agent that serves unlicensed users can quietly consume far more than its prepaid capacity — admins should monitor capacity reports rather than assume a fixed fee covers unlimited custom-agent usage.

term: EU Data Boundary and Microsoft 365 Copilot data processing
def: The EU Data Boundary lets in-scope EU/EFTA customers keep the storage and processing of their Microsoft 365 data — including Copilot prompts, grounding data, and generated responses — within the EU/EFTA region, limiting when that data is transferred outside the boundary.
eg: Enabling the EU Data Boundary is a tenant-wide data-residency commitment, not a Copilot-only toggle, and coverage of specific Copilot experiences has expanded over time — an admin should confirm which particular features are actually in scope rather than assuming everything was covered from day one.

term: Declarative agents vs. custom engine agents in Copilot Studio
def: A declarative agent is built on top of Microsoft 365 Copilot's own orchestrator and Semantic Index, configured mainly through instructions, knowledge sources, and actions with little code. A custom engine agent instead brings its own independent reasoning engine and language model, giving full control at the cost of far more development effort.
eg: An agent created from a SharePoint site is a simple example of a declarative agent, while a fully bespoke agent built with its own model and orchestration logic is a custom engine agent.

term: Microsoft 365 admin center Copilot settings page
def: The Copilot page in the Microsoft 365 admin center is the starting point for tenant-wide Copilot settings, such as enabling or disabling web search (letting Copilot search the public web for extra context; the underlying Allow web search in Copilot policy is configured through the Cloud Policy service), and managing which connectors and agents are available.
eg: This settings page is one of the concrete admin surfaces that makes up the broader Copilot Control System governance umbrella, alongside Purview's data and compliance controls.

def: Classic (topic-based) orchestration follows a fixed set of author-defined conversation topics and trigger phrases to decide how to respond. Generative orchestration instead lets the agent's underlying model dynamically decide, at runtime, which topics, knowledge sources, or actions best answer a given message, reducing how much of every conversation path has to be manually authored.

term: Scoping Conditional Access to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio sign-in
def: Because Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio authenticate through Microsoft Entra, a Conditional Access policy can target them as cloud apps in their own right (for Microsoft 365 Copilot, the Enterprise Copilot Platform service principal, which may first need to be created so it appears in the app picker) — for example, blocking Copilot access from a disallowed country or requiring a compliant device specifically before Copilot sign-in succeeds, without changing sign-in requirements for the rest of Microsoft 365.
eg: This lets an admin apply a narrower rule to Copilot specifically than to Microsoft 365 generally, layering on top of — rather than replacing — the broader Conditional Access policies already governing sign-in.

term: Microsoft 365 Copilot readiness assessment vs. usage reporting
def: A Copilot readiness assessment runs before a rollout, scoring factors like identity hygiene, device compliance, and data governance (oversharing risk) to flag what should be fixed first. Microsoft 365 Copilot usage reporting instead runs after rollout, measuring adoption and active-usage trends once licenses are already assigned.
eg: Treating usage reporting as a stand-in for readiness is a common mistake — a high adoption number after rollout says nothing about whether oversharing or stale permissions were ever actually cleaned up beforehand.

term: Enterprise data protection (EDP) for Copilot Chat
def: When a user signs in with a Microsoft Entra work account, Copilot Chat prompts and responses are protected: encrypted, isolated per tenant, and not used to train foundation models. It also honors permissions, sensitivity labels, retention, and auditing.

term: Third-party AI providers (Anthropic models) in Microsoft Copilot
def: Anthropic is a Microsoft subprocessor, so its Claude models used through Microsoft Copilot, Researcher, Copilot Studio and Copilot in Microsoft 365 apps are covered by the Microsoft DPA, product terms and enterprise data protection. term: Who can use Copilot Cowork: spending policies
def: Access to Cowork is granted only by a spending policy in Copilot > Cost Management that includes the user and selects Cowork, even if the credit limit is tiny. term: Copilot Credits and the Cost management dashboard
def: Copilot Credits are the common unit for usage-based billing of eligible Copilot services. In Copilot > Cost management an admin creates spending policies with a scope (all users or security groups), the agents and services included, limits and alerts, model profiles and a billing method (fixed licensing, pay-as-you-go, prepaid capacity packs or a Copilot Credit Pre-purchase Plan). Auto-apply new services is on by default so new services join existing policies unless it is turned off.

def: End users can request first-time access to a Copilot service or a higher spending limit, and admins act on these in the Credit requests page. Redirected requests still appear in the audit view as Handled externally.

term: Copilot Analytics and the Copilot readiness report
def: Copilot Analytics combines Copilot usage data, agent usage data and Microsoft Graph data, and can add outside business metrics. Operational reports live in the Microsoft 365 admin center, strategic reports (such as the Adoption and Impact tabs) in the Copilot Dashboard in Viva Insights, and agent analytics in the Copilot Studio Analytics tab. A Copilot readiness report in the admin center helps plan licensing and rollout.

term: Secure and governed data foundation blueprint for Copilot
def: Microsoft's blueprint for a Copilot deployment has three pillars: Remediate oversharing, Set up guardrails and Meet regulations. It uses Microsoft Purview and SharePoint Advanced Management (included with a Copilot license) to find high-risk sites, apply interim restrictions where needed, fix access problems and keep guardrails enforced.
eg: Interim restrictions such as Restricted Content Discovery buy time, but the lasting fix is correcting permissions and labeling.

term: Agent registry in the Microsoft 365 admin center
def: Agents > All agents > Registry lists every agent available to the tenant, split into Microsoft agents, external partner-built agents, agents published by your org (line-of-business) and agents shared by their creator. Filters include status, publisher type, channel, platform and data source, and toolbar actions include refresh, export, pinning and customizing the view. An admin can also upload a custom agent manifest as a zip file.
eg: Publisher type answers who owns the agent, platform answers what built it, and channel answers where it is available to users.

def: The registry tracks agents without owners, which appear when the creator of a shared agent is hard-deleted from the tenant, and unmanaged agents, which were created or managed outside Agent 365 and so lack its risk protection and observability. Admins can filter to ownerless agents and block, delete or reassign them. Risk signals from Purview, Entra and Defender are consolidated per agent for tenants with the E7 or Agent 365 license.
eg: Ownerless agents are a lifecycle problem: nobody is accountable for access reviews or retirement, so they are high-priority governance cleanup.

term: Reviewing agent requests: publish or reject
def: Under Agents > All agents > Requests an admin sees agents waiting in states such as Pending review, Pending update and Pending activate. After checking description, owner, data sources, tools and permissions, the admin selects Publish to store (choosing the audience, optional preinstall, a policy template and admin consent for requested permissions) or Reject submission. Until a Pending update is approved, users keep the previous version.
eg: Publishing is scoped, so an approved agent does not have to go to everyone; choose users or groups for a controlled rollout.

term: Agent lifecycle actions: block, delete, activate, install
def: Admin actions on agents include install or uninstall for selected users, activate (limiting who can create instances), block or unblock, delete with a 30-day recovery window (restore or permanently delete), start or stop for Foundry agents, and assign, add or remove owners. Installing requires reviewing the permissions and granting admin consent.
eg: Block stops everyone from using the agent but keeps it in the registry; delete removes it after the recovery window.

def: Agent management rules in Agents > Settings find agents that match conditions, let the admin review them and then apply an action in bulk. Supported scenarios are installing Microsoft agents for everyone, reassigning ownerless Agent Builder agents to the previous owner's manager (from the Entra hierarchy), blocking ownerless agents with no usage, applying a policy template to existing agents (a one-time action) and rejecting publish requests older than a set number of days.
